facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
According to the applicant, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
According to the applicant, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the Turkish intervention in Cyprus.
According to the applicant, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of the missing persons and to protest against human-rights violations.
Photographs 1 to 7 produced by the applicant were intended to show that, notwithstanding the deployment of the Turkish-Cypriot police, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.
In photographs 8 to 10 produced by the applicant, members of the Turkish-Cypriot police are seen breaking up the UNFICYP cordon.
The final set of photographs produced by the applicant show members of the Turkish-Cypriot police using force to arrest some of the women demonstrators.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the applicant made the following statement: 'I consider our arrest as illegal, because we were arrested while we were on a territory which, however you look at it, is Hellenic, by troops we do not recognise. We had come in peace, but were faced by violence, not by the Turkish army, but by the Turkish Cypriots, who until then we had considered as brothers.'

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that some of the other women accused gave statements declaring that the demonstration was peaceful, that they had not carried weapons and that they did not recognise the 'TRNC' as a valid State.
According to the applicant, in the course of the demonstration of 19 July 1989 the applicant was seized by the hair by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.

According to the applicant, in the course of the demonstration of 19 July 1989 the applicant was violently beaten on the head, back and bottom by Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control.

According to the applicant, Turkish military personnel and/or other personnel acting under Turkish control continually grabbed hold of the applicant's breasts during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
According to the applicant, the applicant was dragged to a bus through a crowd that spat and swore at her during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
According to the applicant, the applicant was taken to the so-called 'Pavlides Garage' with other women following the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
On 20 July 1989 the applicant was taken to court and remanded in custody for two days.
The applicant was transferred to Ortakeuy Prison following her court appearance on 20 July 1989.
On 22 July 1989 the court sentenced the applicant to three days' imprisonment.
On 22 July 1989 the court imposed a fine of 50 Cyprus pounds (approximately 85 euros) on the applicant.
The court imposed five additional days in prison on the applicant in default of payment of the fine within 24 hours.
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that the applicant was charged, tried, found guilty and sentenced to a short term of imprisonment.

The English translation of the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 24 other women, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory without permission, contrary to sections 2, 8 and 9 of Law no. 5/72.

The English translation of the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 24 other women, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court concluded, relying on the statements of the prosecution witnesses, that the accused had crossed the borders of the 'TRNC' at an unapproved entry point and without permission and had resisted by various means the UN and Turkish forces which had tried to stop them.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court concluded that the prosecution had proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the accused were guilty on both counts.

In deciding on the sentence, the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court took into account the seriousness of the offence and the fact that the accused had shown no remorse and continued to deny the validity of the 'TRNC'.

The English translation of the 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court judgment of 22 July 1989 indicates that the applicant, together with 24 other women, was charged with entering 'TRNC' territory other than through an approved port, contrary to subsections 12(1) and (5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and such a fine.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators, supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration, were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'TRNC'.
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.

In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by the UN Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) and destroyed a UNFICYP observation post.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 states that a short while later, Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that the witnesses (mainly police officers on duty at the time of the demonstration) declared that the accused had illegally entered the 'TRNC' buffer zone, shouted abuse at the Turkish-Cypriot forces, and resisted arrest by pulling and pushing.
The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court noted that knives and other cutting objects had been found in the bags of some of the demonstrators who had been arrested.

The 'TRNC' Nicosia District Court concluded, relying on the statements of the prosecution witnesses, that the accused had crossed the borders of the 'TRNC' at an unapproved entry point and without permission and had resisted by various means the UN and Turkish forces which had tried to stop them.

According to the applicant, on her arrival at the 'Pavlides Garage' the applicant was searched and forced to sit on the floor.
According to the applicant, the toilet facilities at the 'Pavlides Garage' were filthy and the applicant was refused water.
According to the applicant, two UN soldiers were present at the 'Pavlides Garage' but were not allowed to note down the names of the detainees.
According to the applicant, the crowd outside the 'Pavlides Garage' was swearing, shouting abuse and threats, and throwing stones at the garage, some of which came through the roof.
On 20 July 1989 the applicant was interrogated in the 'Pavlides Garage' for more than an hour.
The applicant refused to sign a statement that was written in Turkish during her interrogation on 20 July 1989.
On 20 July 1989 the applicant was taken to court and remanded in custody for two days.
The applicant was transferred to Ortakeuy Prison following her court appearance on 20 July 1989.
According to the applicant, the conditions of detention at Ortakeuy Prison were appalling and there were not enough beds for all the women detainees.
According to the applicant, during the night at Ortakeuy Prison the applicant and the other detainees were harassed by the guards.
According to the applicant, the applicant had no legal representation at her trial on 21 July 1989.
According to the applicant, the applicant had no proper interpretation at her trial on 21 July 1989.
According to the applicant, the applicant had not previously seen the exhibits which were produced at her trial on 21 July 1989.
According to the applicant, outside the court on 21 July 1989 a crowd had gathered and was constantly shouting.
On 22 July 1989 the court sentenced the applicant to three days' imprisonment.
On 22 July 1989 the court imposed a fine of 50 Cyprus pounds (approximately 85 euros) on the applicant.
The court imposed five additional days in prison on the applicant in default of payment of the fine within 24 hours.
After the trial on 22 July 1989 the applicant was taken back to Ortakeuy Prison.
According to the applicant, in the course of her detention the guards constantly made a lot of noise both during the day and at night.
According to the applicant, in the course of her detention the guards repeatedly entered the cells and turned on the lights.
According to the applicant, on two occasions the applicant had to sign documents written in Turkish in order to get her personal effects back.
According to the applicant, after an incident between the detainees and some Turkish photographers, the applicant was hit by one of her guards and put in an isolation cell.
According to the applicant, the isolation cell was filthy, dark, very hot and had no ventilation.
According to the applicant, while in the isolation cell the applicant was attacked and beaten by one of the guards, receiving severe blows to the face, head and arms.
According to the applicant, the applicant's arm was badly injured and she lost consciousness while in the isolation cell.
According to the applicant, the applicant was visited in the isolation cell by a person claiming to be a doctor who said that she needed treatment, but no treatment was given.
According to the applicant, the applicant remained in the isolation cell until her release on 24 July 1989.
According to the applicant, the applicant was examined by a UN officer who bandaged her arm upon her release on 24 July 1989.
In support of her claim of ill-treatment, the applicant produced two medical certificates.
The first medical certificate was issued by Doctor Andreas Hadjiloizou, a pathologist practising in Ayios Dhometios, on 20 December 2002.

Doctor Andreas Hadjiloizou's certificate states that Mrs Petrakidou visited his clinic on 25 July 1989 after she was released by the Turks and complained of headaches, difficulty in moving her head and pain in the right lower part of the arm following violent twisting.

Doctor Andreas Hadjiloizou's certificate states that examination established that Mrs Petrakidou had mild concussion, difficulty in moving her head and pain in the right lower part of the arm due to violent twisting.
Doctor Andreas Hadjiloizou's certificate states that Mrs Petrakidou was advised to remain in bed for one week.
Doctor Andreas Hadjiloizou's certificate states that Mrs Petrakidou subsequently visited him several times complaining of dizziness and headaches.
The second medical certificate was a 'medical opinion' issued on an unspecified date by Doctor Simos Nissiotis, a specialist orthopaedic surgeon practising in Nicosia.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient Alkiviadous Petrakidou Marianna had been followed by him from 26 July 1989 for various problems resulting from ill-treatment she was subjected to in the prisons of the Turkish-Cypriot pseudo-state in Nicosia.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient participated in an anti-occupation demonstration on 19 July 1989 and was arrested by the authorities of the Turkish-Cypriot pseudo-state.
Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that during her arrest and detention the patient was beaten and ill-treated by the authorities of the Turkish-Cypriot pseudo-state.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient was released on 27 July 1989 and was immediately taken to Nicosia General Hospital to be examined by doctors and to be administered medical treatment.
Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that on 26 July 1989 the patient visited his clinic for further examination and treatment.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient presented with injury to the head and concussion, with diffuse haematomas to the head and mainly in her hair, and was complaining of headache and dizziness, and appeared to be in a very bad shape with a lot of phobias.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient presented with contusion of the nape, complaining of pain and stiffness in the nape with contracted muscles, and that movements of the head were painful and limited and caused aggravation of headache and dizziness.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient presented with contusion of the right forearm, wearing an elastic bandage on her right forearm and complaining mainly of pain with movements in the extensor and flexor, and that upon removal of the bandage she had a haematoma in the area of the round extensor.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that he recommended anti-inflammatory, muscle relaxant and analgesic medicines for the patient's orthopaedic problems, put her forearm in a special sock, and recommended that after the acute phase (approximately 10 days) she start doing exercise and swimming.
Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that for her concussion he recommended that the patient avoid gazing fixedly and exposure to the sun.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient returned to work on 7 August 1989, though still having problems resulting from her contusions and concussion, which decreased in frequency with the passage of time.

Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that the patient has since suffered mainly from pain in the neck, particularly in the cold months, and that this is due to weakness of the muscles of the nape caused by her old injury.
Doctor Simos Nissiotis's medical opinion states that as regards problems resulting from the patient's concussion, phobias and psychological problems, she is being treated by a specialist colleague.
